A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same quality-aware scaling-law research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural machine translation and causal language modeling experiments, including fitted scaling parameters and 63 individual training results per task in Tables 6–7.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds embedding-based semantic-drift measurements and learning-rate sensitivity results in Appendix E.

M1.justification: The scaling equation, quality transformations, model architectures, corruption operators, and fitting objectives remain unchanged. The new deficiency examples and practitioner guide elaborate the existing framework without changing the experimental training or fitting procedure.

E1.justification: Reported coverage remains English–German translation using Paracrawl v8 and English causal language modeling using C4. Appendix E adds diagnostic analyses without introducing another corpus, language, downstream task, or distinct data environment.

E2.justification: The least-squares and Huber fitting comparisons are retained. v2 Table 1 relates the framework mathematically to Chen, Chang, and Goyal; it does not report evaluating these works as additional empirical baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix E adds cosine-similarity evaluation and learning-rate sweeps across dataset scales and noise levels, with batch-size comparisons in Figure 5. Existing training configurations and test splits are unchanged. Sweep reporting is inconsistent: the text specifies five rates, Table 9 lists four, and Figure 5(a) plots six.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds two substantive validation questions absent from v1: whether synthetic corruption tracks semantic degradation, and whether the fitted quality exponent is sensitive to optimization settings. Figures 4–5 and Table 9 provide embedding-drift and learning-rate/batch-size analyses; the original quality-effect analyses remain.

E5.justification: The original three-replicate design and individual-run reporting are retained. The new validations introduce no reported replicate counts, seed specifications, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: All original fitted-parameter entries, 126 individual test losses, and Figures 1–3 are unchanged. Added supporting results include cosine similarity increasing from 0.953 at Q=0.5 to 1.000 at Q=1, and gamma estimates of 0.394 and 0.396 at learning rates 3e-4 and 1e-3. These are new validation outcomes, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix D add a substantial formal extension: deficiency decompositions covering noise, coverage, repetition, and syntheticity, plus dispersion, compression, and epoch-based constructions intended to recover three prior scaling laws. The original lemmas, proposition, and Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: v2 removes the abstract and conclusion statements that the experiments varied coverage, narrowing the empirical claim to synthetic noise variation. The principal contributions and claims about quality-aware scaling, robustness, and model/compute trade-offs remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets embedding similarity as validating the semantic relevance of its quality proxy and describes gamma as stable near practical learning rates. Table 9 identifies extreme settings as undertrained or unstable. The earlier redundancy-based explanation of NMT versus CLM sensitivity is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds a six-step guide for estimating Q, including reference selection, weighted deficiency proxies, validation, and fitting, plus settings for the new sensitivity study. Existing implementation and hardware disclosures are retained. The embedding reference model and analysis sample count remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chen et al. (2025) and substantially expands positioning through Section 4.3, Table 1, and Appendix D. It now argues that its deficiency framework recovers Chen's law and those of previously cited Chang and Goyal, extending beyond v1's qualitative literature discussion.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. Changes include the new comparison subsection and appendices, connecting text, acknowledgments, author/contact formatting, author–year citations, and local wording and notation refinements. The retained narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different document template with narrower text, revised title and heading styles, and substantial resizing and repositioning of existing displays. It adds comparison Table 1, sensitivity Table 9, and Figures 4–5. Figures 1–3 retain identical graphical content.

improvement.justification: Appendix E modestly strengthens empirical support by directly examining corruption semantics and optimization sensitivity, while the narrowed coverage claims better match the experiments. Practical Q-estimation guidance also improves usability. These benefits are limited by incomplete validation details, inconsistent learning-rate counts, and errors in the new theoretical discussion: Appendix D incorrectly states that -ln(1-rho) approaches 1 as rho approaches 0. The revision provides useful additional support without establishing a substantially stronger overall paper.
